_comment: Acids WS2 — DERIVED. No printed key; each answer derived from Class-10 chemistry. REVIEW-prefixed entries are lower-confidence / source-defect items needing human spot-check.

1.reason: Dilute HCl + solid NaHCO3 -> NaCl + H2O + CO2; CO2 escapes as brisk effervescence. No pop sound (that is H2), no black residue.

2.reason: pH 6 (<7) is acidic, pH 8 (>7) is basic. So A is an acid while B is a base.

3.reason: Ca(OH)2, ZnO (amphoteric, reacts as base) and NaOH are bases; sodium sulphate is a (neutral) salt, not a base.

4.reason: Litmus and turmeric are natural indicators; methyl orange and phenolphthalein are synthetic.

5.reason: pH = 0 is the lowest value, a very strong acid -> acidic.

6.reason: A strong base fully dissociates, releasing a large number of OH- ions in solution.

7.reason: Yellow-orange pH paper indicates an acidic soil; to shift it to greenish-blue (basic) add a base. An antacid (mild base) does this; lemon juice and vinegar are acids, common salt is neutral.

8.reason: Antacids (mild bases) neutralise excess stomach acid, treating acidity.

9.reason: Toothpastes are basic to neutralise the acid produced by mouth bacteria.

10.reason: Soap solution is basic; phenolphthalein is pink in basic medium.

11.reason: H2SO4 is diprotic and Mg(OH)2 is diacidic; equal volumes of equal concentration neutralise exactly -> neutral solution -> green with universal indicator.

12.reason: A turns phenolphthalein pink so A is basic; adding B removes pink so B is acidic (neutralises to/below neutral); adding more A makes it pink (basic) again. So basic -> acidic -> basic.

13.reason: Bleaching powder (calcium oxychloride) is a greyish-white (pale yellowish-white) powder with a strong chlorine smell.

14.reason: Acidic strength: water (neutral, weakest) < acetic acid (weak acid) < hydrochloric acid (strong acid).

15.reason: X turns phenolphthalein pink so X is a basic salt = Na2CO3 (only option a has Na2CO3 as X); Y shows no colour change (phenolphthalein colourless in neutral/acidic). Option (a) maps to label A.

16.reason: Washing soda (Na2CO3) is the salt of a strong base (NaOH) and a weak acid (H2CO3) -> a basic salt.

17.reason: Baking soda used in baking is a mixture of sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO3) and a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid.

18.reason: Common to all acids and bases is that both form ions in (aqueous) solution. Not all release the same specific ion.

19.reason: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is wrong: metallic oxides are basic (not acidic) oxides. So (i), (ii) and (iii) only -> label D.

20.reason: NaCl is the salt of a strong acid and strong base -> neutral -> pH = 7.

21.reason: Zn + dilute HCl -> H2 (pop on burning); Zn + dilute NaOH -> H2 as well; NaHCO3 + HCl gives CO2 (no pop). So pairs 1 and 2 = A and B -> label A.

22.reason: Na2CO3 removes permanent hardness (iii) and is used in soda-acid fire extinguishers (ii); CaOCl2 (bleaching powder) disinfects water (i); CaSO4.1/2H2O (Plaster of Paris) makes toys/decoration (iv). Matching (a)-iii,(b)-ii,(c)-i,(d)-iv -> label B.

23.reason: Glucose and alcohol are non-electrolytes (no ions, bulb does not glow); HCl and H2SO4 are strong acids that ionise and conduct -> bulb glows.

24.reason: Marble, limestone and baking soda are carbonates/bicarbonate that release CO2 with dilute acid; lime (CaO) is an oxide and does not give CO2.

25.reason: A normal salt of a strong acid and strong base is neutral, pH = 7.

26.reason: CuO + 2HCl -> CuCl2 + H2O; copper(II) chloride solution is blue-green.

27.reason: Anhydrous CaCl2 is a drying agent; it absorbs moisture from the HCl gas in the guard tube.

28.reason: Lime (lemon) juice is acidic (citric acid). Lime water and antacids are basic; blood is slightly basic.

29.reason: Egg shells (CaCO3) react with an acid to give CO2, which turns lime water milky. Only HCl is an acid among the options.

30.reason: Always add concentrated acid to water (slowly, with stirring) so the heat is dissipated; adding water to acid can cause violent spattering.

31.reason: Oxalic acid (acidic) turns pH paper orange/red; sodium carbonate (basic) turns it blue. So A = orange, B = blue.

32.reason: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is the acid secreted in the stomach.

33.reason: Vanilla essence has an odour that disappears in basic solution, so a visually-impaired student can use it as an olfactory acid-base indicator.

34.reason: Bleaching powder is made by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime, Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 -> CaOCl2 + H2O.

35.reason: Tooth enamel begins to corrode (decay starts) when mouth pH falls below 5.5; 5.8 is the closest option.

36.reason: An acid reacts with a carbonate (Na2CO3) to give salt + water + CO2. PbSO4, AgCl and Na2SO4 do not react with dilute acid this way.

37.reason: Adding a small amount of acid to water causes ionization (1) and dilution (3). No base present so no neutralization or salt formation. -> (i) and (iii), label A.

38.reason: Tomato contains oxalic acid. (Ant/nettle sting = formic/methanoic acid; tamarind = tartaric acid.)

39.reason: Antacids treat indigestion/acidity by neutralising excess stomach acid.

40.reason: Mg(OH)2 (milk of magnesia) is a mild base used as an antacid; NaCl is neutral, H2SO4 and HCl are acids.

41.reason: Aqua regia (3:1 conc. HCl : conc. HNO3) dissolves gold.

42.reason: Propanoic acid (C2H5COOH) is the only acid; acids turn blue litmus red. The aldehyde, ketone and alcohol are not acidic.

43.reason: Plaster of Paris (CaSO4.1/2H2O) sets/hardens by combining with water to form gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O).

44.reason: NaHCO3 reacts with acetic acid giving sodium acetate + water + CO2; the solid dissolves and a clear solution with brisk effervescence is obtained.

45.reason: Acetic acid + sodium bicarbonate (X) gives CO2 (Y), which turns lime water milky. So X = sodium bicarbonate, Y = CO2.

46.reason: REVIEW: Dilute NaOH is a base, so it shows none of properties 1, 3, 4 (acid behaviours) and turns turmeric red (basic property, statement 2). Only statement (ii) applies; the printed option b reads '(ii) and (ii) only' (typo) but is the only option containing (ii). Marking B as the intended answer; verify the source option text.

48.reason: NaOH is basic; phenolphthalein turns pink in a basic solution.

49.reason: Gypsum (CaSO4.2H2O), Epsom salt (MgSO4.7H2O), blue vitriol (CuSO4.5H2O) and Glauber's salt (Na2SO4.10H2O) all contain water of crystallization -> all four (A, B, C and D), label B.

50.reason: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate, Na2CO3.10H2O.

51.reason: HCl + Na2CO3 -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2; carbon dioxide is liberated.

53.reason: Dilution of a concentrated acid in water releases a large amount of heat -> exothermic.

54.reason: Lime water is a solution of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2.

55.reason: Heating gypsum to ~373 K gives Plaster of Paris (CaSO4.1/2H2O), which sets into a HARD mass with water; option B (sets into a 'liquid mass') is the INCORRECT statement asked for. (Note: option D, calling it dihydrate, is also factually wrong, but B is the clearly intended incorrect statement about setting.)

56.reason: Acidic strength: sodium chloride (neutral salt) < acetic acid (weak acid) < hydrochloric acid (strong acid).

57.reason: REVIEW: Soda lime is commonly stated as NaOH : CaO in a definite ratio, but the options are odd decimal numbers with no clear standard value (common references quote roughly 3:1 NaOH:CaO by mass). None of the printed decimals (0.0854, 0.1257, 0.04375, 0.1264) matches a standard textbook ratio; the source/key is unclear. Tentatively marking A; human verification required against the source.

58.reason: Bleaching powder is used as a bleaching agent in the paper (and textile) industry.

59.reason: NaOH, KOH and NH4OH are bases; C2H5OH (ethanol) is an alcohol, not a base.

60.reason: The pH scale measures the hydrogen-ion concentration of a solution.

62.reason: NaCl and Na2SO4 are both sodium salts (the family is defined by the common cation Na+).

63.reason: HNO3 is a strong acid because it dissociates completely into ions in aqueous solution.

64.reason: Egg shells (CaCO3) react with an acid to release CO2 (turns lime water milky). Only HCl is an acid among LiCl, KCl, HCl, NaCl.

65.reason: pH = 13 is well above 7, indicating a strongly basic solution.

66.reason: Phenolphthalein is pink only in basic solutions (pH > 7). R (pH 9) and S (pH 13) are basic; P (2) and Q (7) are not -> R and S, label A.

67.reason: Citric acid is an organic acid; nitric, sulphuric and hydrochloric acids are mineral (inorganic) acids.

68.reason: Al2O3 is amphoteric: it reacts with HCl (as a base) and with KOH (as an acid) to give salt and water. Na2O and K2O are basic, CuO is basic.

69.reason: Limestone (CaCO3) decomposes on heating to give CaO + CO2. Quick lime (CaO), slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) and soda ash (Na2CO3) do not readily give CO2 on heating.

70.reason: As pH rises from 7 to 14 the solution becomes more basic, i.e. the concentration of OH- ions increases. (Option A is the correctly-worded choice; option D, increase in H3O+, is wrong.)

71.reason: Sodium carbonate (washing soda), Na2CO3.10H2O, removes permanent hardness of water by precipitating Ca2+/Mg2+ as carbonates.

72.reason: Bleaching powder reacts with CO2 (and moisture) to form calcium carbonate and release chlorine: CaOCl2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + Cl2. (Option a text appears mis-printed; D is the correct chemistry.)

73.reason: An aqueous solution of NH3 (ammonium hydroxide) is basic and turns red litmus blue. Dry NH3 and dry HCl have no effect on dry litmus; aqueous HCl is acidic.

74.reason: HCl is a strong acid because it dissociates fully, giving a large number of H+ ions in solution.

75.reason: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2; a colourless, odourless gas (hydrogen) evolves with bubbles.

47.reason: Heating hydrated blue copper sulphate drives off the water of crystallization: CuSO4.5H2O (blue) -> CuSO4 (white) + 5H2O. So statement 1 (white residue) and statement 2 (water droplets condense on the cooler upper part of the tube) are both correct. Statement 3 is wrong: adding water to the white anhydrous residue turns it back BLUE, not green. Hence I and II only -> option D.
